one_liner: SwiftUI-style browser UI framework in Swift compiled to WebAssembly; 1.14x faster than React 19 hooks overall, all from swap rows.
what_it_does: Brings the declarative HTML DSL of Elementary (a server-side Swift HTML renderer) to apps that run in the browser as WebAssembly. Views are @View structs with a `var body`, state lives in @State, @Environment and @Reactive classes, lists use ForEach(items, key:), and an app starts with Application(App()).mount(in: "#app"); there are also CSS/FLIP animations, transitions and an optional ElementaryWebComponents module that publishes views as custom elements. It is a different language and API from React, not a drop-in; builds go through the swift.org Swift SDKs for WebAssembly plus a Vite plugin (@elementary-swift/vite-plugin-swift-wasm).
how_it_is_fast: Views are ahead-of-time compiled Swift (optionally Embedded Swift for a smaller module), and state changes are tracked by a Reactivity module modelled on Swift's Observation framework, so updates are queued and run in one microtask-scheduled cycle that separates reconciliation from a batched DOM commit phase. Keyed lists are diffed by KeyedDiffEngine: it trims the unchanged prefix and suffix, takes fast paths for pure insertions and deletions, and uses a longest-increasing-subsequence (LIS) pass to move only the out-of-order nodes, which is why swapping two rows costs 14.7 ms against React hooks' 89.7 ms. DOM calls still cross the Wasm-to-JavaScript boundary through JavaScriptKit, so creation-heavy work is slower than in the JS frameworks.
when_to_use: A team that already writes Swift (server-side Elementary/Hummingbird/Vapor or Apple apps) and wants browser UI in the same language with SwiftUI-like syntax.
Keyed lists that are frequently reordered or have rows moved: the LIS-based diff beats React 19 hooks by about 6x on the suite's swap-rows test (14.7 vs 89.7 ms).
Large one-shot table builds and clears where it measured slightly ahead of React hooks (create 10,000 rows 349.6 vs 401.0 ms; clear 16.1 vs 17.6 ms).
Shipping Swift-written widgets into an existing site as custom elements via ElementaryWebComponents.
when_not_to_use: When raw DOM speed is the goal: in the same run it takes 1.6x vanilla JS's time and 1.26-1.45x Vue 3.5, Svelte 5 and Solid 1.9, and is slower than the Rust Wasm frameworks Leptos, Dioxus and Sycamore (1.23-1.28x their time) (unweighted geometric means derived from page data).

Typical CRUD rendering against React: excluding swap rows it takes 1.081x React hooks' time and is slower on 5 of 9 tests (create 1,000 rows 31.9 vs 23.6 ms, append 38.1 vs 29.3 ms, replace all 36.9 vs 30.2 ms).

Load-time-sensitive pages: first paint 815.9 vs 226.6 ms for React, compressed size 143.7 vs 51.4 kB and uncompressed 720.4 vs 190.3 kB (a 666 KB .wasm plus a 55 KB JS loader in the benchmark bundle).
Sites with a strict Content-Security-Policy: the suite flags the implementation with note 1139 (does not pass its strict same-origin CSP).

Projects that need API stability: the README calls it 'an actively developed passion project in its early days', and 0.7.0 and 0.8.0 both shipped breaking changes (runtime removal and a Swift 6.4 minimum).

integration.form: Swift package (SwiftPM library products ElementaryUI and ElementaryWebComponents) compiled to a .wasm module and bundled by Vite
integration.dependencies: JavaScriptKit (0.59.x), elementary 0.8.2+, swift-collections 1.7.1+ with the UnstableContainersPreview and UnstableHashedContainers traits, swift-syntax 600-604 for the macros; at build time Node, Vite and @elementary-swift/vite-plugin-swift-wasm
integration.min_toolchain: Swift 6.4 or later with the matching swift.org Swift SDK for WebAssembly (required since 0.8.0); package manifest uses swift-tools-version 6.4 and experimental features (Lifetimes, RawLayout, BuiltinModule, Extern)
integration.platforms: Browsers with WebAssembly (wasm32), built either with the Embedded Swift SDK (small module) or the full Swift SDK; benchmarked in Chrome 154 on Apple M4
integration.thread_safety: Single-threaded browser main-thread model; the README lists 'isolation and @MainActor stuff for reusable types' as unresolved

gotchas: The headline win over React hooks rests on one test: the 0.877x unweighted geometric mean becomes 1.081x (slower) once swap rows, React hooks' known weak spot, is removed; ElementaryUI is also slower than every Rust Wasm sibling in the same run except near-parity with Yew (1.071x).

The benchmark implementation in krausest/js-framework-benchmark was written and version-bumped by the ElementaryUI author (sliemeobn commits 6b79cfb, 0e53da5, 5cdcee2), and the suite runs a prebuilt bundled-dist (build-prod is a no-op) whose Swift 6.4+ toolchain version and optimisation flags are not recorded; the results page is a development snapshot (isOfficial = false). The implementation itself follows the suite's rules (swapAt(1, 998), ' !!!' on every 10th row, 'danger' class on select).

Embedded Swift limits: KeyedDiffEngine.swift notes that 'Hashing a stored view key traps on the embedded Wasm target', the README says Codable/JSON is not available in Embedded Swift yet, and the benchmark build sets linkEmbeddedUnicodeDataTables: false while its Row == compares label.utf8 bytes instead of String equality, so Unicode-aware string handling in an app may need the tables linked and a larger bundle (inference from the config; size impact not measured).

Strict-CSP failure (suite note 1139): the bundled JS loader contains no eval or new Function but instantiates WebAssembly via instantiateStreaming, so the cause is probably that compiling Wasm needs 'wasm-unsafe-eval' (inference; the issue page does not say).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it over Leptos, Dioxus, Sycamore or Yew only when the codebase is Swift rather than Rust; in the same Chrome 154 run those Rust Wasm frameworks are 7-28% faster by geometric mean and ship smaller first paint, so on speed alone they win.
verified_claims_summary: In krausest/js-framework-benchmark's Chrome 154 development snapshot (Apple M4, macOS 26.6.2), elementaryui-v0.8.0-keyed (Embedded Swift build) against react-hooks-v19.2.0-keyed median totals were: swap 14.7 vs 89.7 ms, create 10k 349.6 vs 401.0, clear 16.1 vs 17.6, remove 11.3 vs 11.3, select 5.7 vs 5.4, partial update 15.2 vs 14.7, replace 36.9 vs 30.2, append 38.1 vs 29.3, create 1k 31.9 vs 23.6 ms. I recomputed the unweighted geometric mean from results.ts: 0.877x React's time (1.081x without swap) and 1.597x vanilla JS's time (derived from page data). The project itself makes no speed claim.
status_note: Actively developed (0.8.0 released 29 Sep 2026, last commit 2026-10-09, 511 stars) and Apache-2.0, but pre-1.0 with breaking changes in recent minors and a Swift 6.4 minimum; usable for Swift-first teams, not a performance upgrade over the fast JS or Rust frameworks.
